title: Fleeing yourself
hookLine: restless people keep changing places, fleeing themselves (On Tranquility 2)

lines: EACH POSITION SEEMS LIKE THE ANSWER.
cards: Seneca's picture comes from a bad night. Left side, too warm. Flip the pillow.
Right side. Then the back. Each new position seems like the answer, briefly.
In the second chapter of On Tranquility, he stops listening to Serenus' symptoms and starts naming the illness.
Restless people, he says, behave like the sleepless: they keep turning over, trying one position after another, until they finally settle from exhaustion rather than rest.

teach.b: First, the root. The trouble, Seneca says, is a quiet dislike of yourself. Not hatred.
More like boredom with your own company. A mind that can't settle with itself goes looking for somewhere else to be. Second, the trips.
Seneca sketches the restless Roman: let's go to the seaside. No, too much luxury there; let's see the wild hills. No, too rough; back to the city, I've missed the noise.
Every move is a new position in bed. Third, the poet's line.
Seneca quotes the Roman poet Lucretius, in a line of Latin: hoc se quisque modo fugit. Thus each person flees himself. Then his own sharp question: but what good does it do, if you can't escape?

You go along as your own companion, the very one you're running from. Back on day four hundred fifty-seven, a letter said you take yourself along. The essay goes one step further: the running is itself the symptom.
Fourth, the cure begins with stopping. Seneca will offer remedies in the coming chapters, work, friends, simplicity, rest, but none of them work while you're still fleeing.
The first move is the unglamorous one: stay put, and get to know the person you keep trying to leave behind. Other paths keep their own version.
Among the early Christian desert monks, a saying credited to Abba Moses told a restless brother to sit in his cell, and the cell would teach him everything.

how: People following Seneca's advice sometimes practice staying in one place, doing one thing, for a set time, to notice the urge to flee without obeying it.

o: hiding your true feelings from other people
changing places to escape your own company
running away from home to start a new life

s: Seneca says a new place is the best cure for restlessness
he says you take yourself along; the running is the symptom.
Seneca quotes the poet Lucretius on fleeing oneself
hoc se quisque modo fugit: thus each person flees himself.
Seneca roots restlessness in hating other people
he roots it in a quiet dislike of, or boredom with, yourself.

games.q: you're awake at night, turning from side to side. in Seneca's picture, how does the sleepless person finally settle?
o: by getting up and leaving town.
games.why: Seneca says they settle at last from weariness: that's where endless changing leads, and he says the restless do the same with places.

practice: For these two minutes, don't change position at all; when an itch comes, or the urge to check something, or the thought that this is boring, notice it, and stay.
You're keeping company with the one person you can't leave, so be a polite host, and ask gently: what are you hoping to get away from?

wordCard.voice: Fleeing yourself. In Seneca's essay, the restless keep changing places, like a sleepless person turning over, and take themselves everywhere they go. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, Lucretius quoted by Seneca: 'thus each person flees himself'.

carryVoice: Your line: stay put. Wherever you go, you come along too. Day four hundred ninety-six, done.
